hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
Your daily step count and resting heart rate may offer clues to how fast you age.

People who averaged fewer than 5,000 steps a day were more likely to show a pace of aging above 1.2 biological years per calendar year. That’s more than 14 months of biological aging in 12 months. People with a resting heart rate above 80 beats per minute were also more likely to show accelerated biological aging.

On the other hand, each additional 3,000 daily steps and a resting heart rate 10 beats per minutes lower were associated with an estimated 11 fewer days of biological aging per year.

When I spoke with Dr. Steve Horvath (@prof_horvath), we discussed how researchers use DunedinPACE to test whether lifestyle changes can slow the pace of aging. What stands out in this study is that two numbers you can check on your wrist tracked with signs of aging that researchers could detect in your DNA!
hits.draft_en:
Rhonda Patrick shared research tying your daily steps and resting heart rate to how fast you age.

People under 5,000 steps a day were more likely to age biologically faster than the calendar. A resting heart rate over 80 was the same story. Roughly every extra 3,000 steps, and a resting heart rate 10 beats lower, lined up with about 11 fewer days of biological ageing per year.

Over 50 on a worksite, you don't need a fancy watch. Walk more on your breaks, climb the stairs, and keep an eye on that resting pulse in the morning.

Why do testosterone levels appear to be declining among men?

I think a few reasons...

Too little sleep can lower testosterone. Diet may play a role, too, especially if you’re eating a lot of refined sugar and processed foods or getting too little zinc and magnesium. Zinc, for example, helps the body make testosterone.

What concerns me is that these chemicals can interfere with how hormones work. That includes sex hormones like testosterone and estrogen, as well as thyroid hormones, which help regulate metabolism.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Blood glucose that swings up and down can harm blood vessels more than glucose that stays high.

Most of the attention goes to how high glucose gets, and that does matter. Higher glucose impairs the lining of blood vessels, and the higher it goes, the worse that lining works.

A controlled human experiment tested what happens when glucose comes and goes. Healthy adults and adults with type 2 diabetes had their glucose held steadily high for a full day in one condition, and pushed up and down between normal and high every few hours in another. Glucose that kept rising and falling impaired blood vessel function more than glucose held steady, even at the top of that range. Markers of oxidative stress followed the same pattern. Giving vitamin C at the same time reversed the impairment, which points to oxidative stress as the cause.

The lining of a blood vessel controls how well the vessel widens, largely through nitric oxide. Each rapid rise in glucose pushes cells to make more reactive oxygen molecules, and those molecules break down nitric oxide. Repeating that rise again and again appears to keep the cells from adjusting.

This matters because fasting glucose and A1C reflect averages. Two people can have the same A1C while one has steady glucose and the other goes up and down after every high-carbohydrate meal and snack. A continuous glucose monitor shows those swings in a way a single lab value can't.

Dietary carbohydrate, especially the refined, fast-digesting kind, is the main driver of those swings. Meals built on protein and fat raise glucose very little.

If someone wants to protect their blood vessels, it's worth paying attention to how much their glucose moves through the day, along with where the average sits.
hits.draft_en:
Ben Bikman on blood sugar that swings up and down.

In a controlled experiment, healthy adults and people with type 2 diabetes had glucose held steadily high for a day, or pushed up and down every few hours. The swinging glucose damaged blood vessel function more than the steady high. Oxidative stress markers followed the same pattern.

Fasting glucose and A1C are averages — they can hide the spikes. Over 50, ask about how much your glucose moves through the day, not just the average.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
High cholesterol doesn’t automatically mean high heart disease risk — not if you’re fit.

A 2022 study of 8,920 men with hypercholesterolemia (no prior heart disease or cancer) from the Cooper Clinic followed them for an average of 17 years. Researchers measured cardiorespiratory fitness with maximal treadmill testing and looked at cardiovascular death rates.

After adjusting for age, BMI, total cholesterol level itself, smoking, blood pressure, diabetes, and other factors, the results were clear:

• Moderate fitness → 34% lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease
• High fitness → 45% lower risk
compared with the least-fit men.

In other words, the protective effect of fitness held even after accounting for the elevated cholesterol numbers. Higher fitness substantially reduced cardiovascular mortality risk independent of the cholesterol reading.

This aligns with a larger body of evidence showing that cardiorespiratory fitness is one of the strongest predictors of longevity and often attenuates or overrides risks tied to traditional markers like high cholesterol or higher body weight.

The takeaway is practical: improving fitness (through consistent aerobic training and overall physical activity) can meaningfully lower risk, even when cholesterol is elevated. Numbers on a lab report are only part of the picture — capacity matters.

Your Plants Are Stealing Your Minerals

Phytic acid (phytate) is the main storage form of phosphorus in grains, legumes, nuts, and seeds. It also happens to be one of the most effective mineral-binding compounds in the human diet.

A quantitative model by Hambidge and colleagues (updated with human absorption data) shows the effect clearly:
•  With essentially zero phytate, the Estimated Average Requirement for zinc is about 9 mg/day for men and 7 mg/day for women.
•  Add 1,000 mg of phytate per day and the requirement roughly doubles.
•  Add 2,000 mg and it roughly triples.
At phytate-to-zinc molar ratios above ~11:1 (men) or ~15:1 (women), it becomes difficult or impossible to meet physiologic zinc needs no matter how much zinc is in the food. High-phytate diets (common with unrefined grains and legumes) regularly hit these ratios.

Phytate doesn’t stop at zinc. It forms insoluble complexes with iron, calcium, magnesium, and other divalent minerals. Calcium makes the problem worse for zinc by creating even less soluble calcium-zinc-phytate complexes. Oxalates (spinach, almonds, etc.) do the same to calcium. Tannins (tea, coffee, legumes) further suppress non-heme iron absorption. The net result is that the more plant foods you eat as staples, the higher your actual mineral requirements become — and the lower the fraction you actually absorb.

Animal foods contain negligible phytate, negligible oxalate, and negligible tannins. The minerals in meat, organs, and dairy arrive without these built-in inhibitors. This is one reason traditional cultures that relied heavily on grains developed soaking, fermenting, and sprouting techniques: they were trying to degrade the anti-nutrients that modern food guidelines largely ignore.
The data are straightforward. The more phytate you eat, the more zinc (and other minerals) you need to get the same amount absorbed. Or you can just eat food that doesn’t contain the inhibitor in the first place.

In 1985, two researchers dissected 202 mammals and measured their fat cells. What they found was simple and hard to ignore.

Decades later, this observation was cited in the Ben-Dor, Sirtoli & Barkai review on the human trophic level as one of the physiological markers placing ancestral humans with carnivores — alongside stomach acidity, early weaning, and others.
Your fat cells don’t care about food pyramids. They still look like they belong to a meat-eater.

hits.text:
Large fat cells predict type 2 diabetes better than total body fat does. Adults with normal glucose tolerance had a small sample of belly fat taken and were followed for years. The people whose fat cells were largest at the start were far more likely to develop diabetes, even after accounting for how much body fat they carried and how insulin resistant they already were.

Fat cells that grow very large struggle to store more fat safely, so more fat spills toward the liver, muscle and pancreas.

If someone is trying to judge their metabolic risk, how their fat is stored can tell more than how much of it they carry.

I USED TO TAKE 2 NEXIUM EVERY SINGLE DAY

Early in my career, I put people with reflux on the highest-dose acid blocker and told them they'd be on it for life. I was taking 2 Nexium every single day myself.

A randomized trial assigned 98 veterans with reflux to 4 diets for 9 weeks. The group that kept total carbs high but cut simple sugars by about 62 grams a day had a fall in measured acid exposure, while the control group had a rise.

I should have asked more about what people were eating before telling them they needed a pill for life.

If you need an acid blocker every day, review your food and your medicine with your doctor. Don't stop a prescribed medicine on your own.
